Slight positive benefit up to ~$15M of pressure
Low-to-mid single-digit scanner data minus ~$15M conservative inventory assumption
Q3 revenue fell 31% to $265.7M, primarily due to ~$124M of distributor (Pepsi) inventory optimization; YTD revenue still grew 5% to $1.02B.

Celsius retail sales rose 7.1% (units +7.3%) overcoming a category that grew only 2%; Celsius contributed >16% of all category growth - management framed retail performance as resilient despite the reported revenue collapse.

Profitability cratered: Q3 gross margin 46% (vs 50.4% PY), adjusted EBITDA down 96% to ~$4.4M, net income down 92% to ~$6.4M - but YTD figures are 'more indicative of full-year operations' (YTD gross margin 50.2%, EBITDA $192.8M).

Two margin pressures: the ~$124M Pepsi inventory optimization and the new Pepsi incentive program (priority periods, aligned resources) that fully ramped in Q3; partially offset by reduced outbound freight and material savings.

Management characterized Q3 optimization as 'very good' and 'very efficient' (the distributor commented on it on its own call); Q4 is more a function of where the category goes than further optimization.

Q4 guidance: a range from a slight positive benefit up to ~$15M of pressure; sell-in and sell-through should align before Q4 ends; Q4 NA growth modelable as low-to-mid single-digit scanner data minus a conservative ~$15M inventory assumption.
Three reiterated growth drivers: attracting new consumers, expanding product availability, increasing consumption frequency.

Q3 was 'troubled with traffic' - major retailers cited reduced convenience traffic; the shopper is taking one less trip/occasion; management needs traffic and occasions to return and macro trends to improve.

Celsius's share is historically stronger in food/drug/mass and on Amazon than in convenience; closing the convenience gap is the big opportunity (better placements, path-to-purchase disruption, higher household penetration).

Sugar-free crossed >50% of the category for the first time; the Better-For-You / performance-energy / fitness-lifestyle secular trend continues; competitors (Red Bull, Monster) leaning into sugar-free reinforces the opportunity.

Big Beverage co-packer acquisition: a capital-efficient vertical-integration move (LTOs, innovation, Orbit-model optimization); the plant predominantly ran Celsius; management does NOT intend to become a co-packer and prefers staying asset-light.

International revenue grew 37% to $18.6M; Australia and New Zealand launched (7-Eleven partner); UK/Ireland with Suntory and Tesco; a new Ireland center of excellence (supply chain, innovation, marketing) being stood up to enable faster scaled global expansion; expansion pace tempered to consumer acceptance.
Management explicitly is not providing formal forward guidance (could reevaluate in future); declined to commit on the international ramp magnitude.

Catalysts: Jake Paul/Mike Tyson Netflix event title sponsorship (within ~2 weeks; potentially the largest live boxing event in history); positive NACS retailer feedback for 2025 resets; Supplier of the Year awards at 7-Eleven, Circle K and Casey's; KDP/Ghost deal seen as creating disruption-driven opportunity.
Pricing: Celsius rolled out a price increase but is 'being conservative' and does not expect significant benefit in 2025; has not disclosed the amount; Monster took a Nov 1 list-price increase.
Should scanner-data trends improve sequentially month-on-month through Q4 into 2025, and what would need to change in the consumer to reaccelerate category growth in 2025?

Fieldly: Q4 has a variety of planned promotional activities amid a highly promotional category and heavy competitor innovation; a Jake Paul/Mike Tyson title sponsorship for national reach. On reacceleration: Q3 was 'troubled with traffic' - the company needs convenience traffic and occasions to return; the Better-For-You/performance-energy/fitness-lifestyle position has tailwinds; the category crossed 50% sugar-free; macro trends need to improve, and management is confident the category will return to growth.
Details on the new Pepsi incentive structure and why it drives category acceleration; and is the distributor inventory optimization done?

Fieldly: the alignment incentive program is being further implemented into 2025 with additional focus and priority periods, with strong cross-functional collaboration after NACS and Pepsi's AOP meeting. Langhans: management has a handful of weeks of Q4 visibility and sees a tighter weekly correlation between sell-in and depletions vs Q3; a slight disconnect remains but sell-in and sell-through should align before Q4 ends; guided Q4 to a range from a slight positive benefit up to ~$15M of pressure - November and December are key.
How to benchmark the inventory destock/restock outcome against scanner demand trends, and where has the consumer that drove the May share peak gone?

Langhans: the scanner-demand framing is good - if trends pick up Celsius has a better opportunity to benefit; flat means nothing substantial. Fieldly: the share decline since the May peak reflects convenience-channel expansion challenges and foot-traffic weakness (shoppers taking one less trip/occasion); competitor innovation also expanded trial; confident in the portfolio, 2025 innovation, and positive NACS retailer feedback, citing the deepening third-year Pepsi relationship.
Is Celsius's share weaker in convenience stores than in mass, Amazon and Costco?

Fieldly confirmed: historically Celsius's share has been better in food/drug/mass and on Amazon than in convenience - so closing the convenience gap is the big opportunity, requiring better placements, path-to-purchase disruption and higher household penetration; the sugar-free/Better-For-You/fitness-lifestyle consumer is there and Celsius is well positioned when the category returns to growth.

Will the Q4 inventory assumption be updated through the quarter, what underpins the $15M headwind, how does visibility compare to spring/summer, and can 4Q NA growth be modeled as scanner data minus an inventory assumption?

Langhans: visibility is good and teams are working closer together; Q3's optimization was very efficient (the distributor commented on it); Q4 is more a function of where the category goes than further optimization; the $15M range is a trend-based analysis. He confirmed ('Yes') that Q4 NA growth can be modeled as low-to-mid single-digit scanner data minus a conservative ~$15M inventory assumption.
What is genuinely different in Celsius's plans vs peers doing similar promotions and innovation, and should investors brace for YoY share declines if sequential share holds?

Fieldly: share involves many variables (shopping-pattern changes, innovation, sentiment). Celsius has tactics to drive new-to-category consumption (Gen Z/college program), leverage the Better-For-You/sugar-free movement, and increase availability via deeper Pepsi alignment and cooler placements; increased-consumption occasions include foodservice; national reach from the Jake Paul/Tyson Netflix event; new flavor innovation reinforces the 'most refreshing' positioning.
Has management considered introducing formal guidance, and is there a case to expand internationally much more aggressively to offset US deceleration with the right leadership in place?

Fieldly: many variables in the models - 'at this time, the company is not providing forward guidance' (could reevaluate). On international: multiple 2024 expansions announced (Suntory UK/Ireland; Australia, New Zealand, France); agrees the opportunities are large but is 'being very cognizant of timing and sequencing' and will 'temper expectations,' moving as fast as the brand gains acceptance. Langhans: standing up a center of excellence (supply chain, innovation, marketing) to enable faster scaled global expansion.
Kevin Grundy (BNP Paribas) / Michael Lavery (Piper Sandler)
How much of 2025 shelf space is already set, how does Celsius position competitively against Ghost/KDP, and how will Celsius deploy its large cash balance after Big Beverage?

Fieldly: NACS feedback was positive, giving confidence Celsius will gain additional shelf space, better placements and secondary cold placements in 2025; won Supplier of the Year awards at 7-Eleven, Circle K and Casey's. KDP/Ghost reinforces the performance-energy/Better-For-You opportunity, and disruption creates opportunity. On capital: an extremely healthy balance sheet; Big Beverage adds flexibility for LTOs/innovation/Orbit-model optimization with good ROI. Langhans: Big Beverage was a plant predominantly running Celsius, easy to absorb - but Celsius does not desire to become a co-packer and prefers staying asset-light.
How does the execution playbook evolve for 2025 given Red Bull's and Monster's sugar-free pushes, and has Celsius communicated anything to the trade on pricing given Monster's Nov 1 increase?

Fieldly: Red Bull's and Monster's sugar-free leaning-in reinforces Celsius's opportunity as a strong #3 player and the broader sugar-free/Better-For-You movement; increased competition allows further expansion. The 2025 playbook returns to the three growth drivers (new-to-category Gen Z/coffee-occasion replacement, increased availability via Pepsi alignment, increased consumption via foodservice/Jersey Mike's). On pricing: Celsius rolled out a price increase but is 'being cognizant' and does not expect significant benefit in 2025; has not disclosed the amount - 'we're being conservative on that.'
